title: Sharp graph-removal bounds for fixed patterns
formal: Determine the asymptotic order of the extremal copy-count function \(M_H(\varepsilon,n)\) defined below, for every fixed connected finite simple graph \(H\) with at least two edges. Both the proximity parameter \(\varepsilon\) and the graph order \(n\) vary. The requested precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(H\), uniformly over all feasible pairs \((\varepsilon,n)\). Thus the answer must specify bounds \(B_H(\varepsilon,n)>0\) and prove that, for each such \(H\), there are constants \(0<c_H\le C_H<\infty\) such that \[c_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\le M_H(\varepsilon,n)\le C_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\] for every feasible pair. The copies are ordinary subgraphs, with extra edges allowed.
why: Removal bounds quantify how visible a forbidden configuration must become once a graph is globally far from avoiding it. Their dependence on the distance parameter controls the sampling cost of detecting violations and connects dense-graph testing to extremal and additive combinatorics. Distinguishing polynomial from superpolynomial dependence identifies a broad boundary, but does not determine the rate on either side of it.
status_note: The source poses this quantitative target in 2017. The source definitions, Fox’s logarithmic-height tower bound, the minimum-degree restriction in Fox–Wigderson, the 2025 survey and the 2025 hypergraph classification were checked on 15 September 2026. A bounded search of later work did not identify matching general bounds; this is not an exhaustive certification of openness or an independent verification of the cited proofs. Constant-factor precision, the subset-copy convention and the feasible-domain treatment are recorded editorial specifications.

progress.text: The graph-removal theorem supplies a positive density guarantee, while the ordinary subgraph-freeness dichotomy distinguishes bipartite patterns, which have polynomial bounds, from nonbipartite patterns, which do not. This is a classification of the broad rate regime, not matching bounds for every pattern.

Fox's Theorem 1 improves the general removal guarantee to an inverse tower of twos whose height is \(O_H(\log(1/\varepsilon))\), after translating distance and copy conventions. This is an upper bound on the required reciprocal density; it is not a matching construction showing that tower growth is necessary.
Goldreich poses the connected-pattern copy-count question as Open Problem 8.17 and summarizes available bounds in Theorem 8.18; footnote 41 records the logarithmic-height tower improvement.

Fox–Wigderson prove linear clique-removal bounds under a minimum degree greater than \((2r-5)n/(2r-3)\) by a fixed positive fraction of \(n\), for the pattern \(K_r\). Below that threshold they recover superpolynomial behavior. The additional minimum-degree hypothesis is absent from the general target.

Gishboliner–Shapira settle the higher-uniformity analogue of the polynomial-removal classification: ordinary hypergraph removal has polynomial bounds precisely for partite patterns. That result does not give matching growth bounds for the nonbipartite graph cases here.

The Polynomial Property Testing survey retains the polynomial/nonpolynomial dichotomy in Section 3.1. A bounded later-work search on 15 September 2026 did not identify matching general bounds for the full copy-count target.

sentences: For each fixed connected graph pattern, the question asks how few ordinary copies a graph can contain while still being far from avoiding that pattern.
Distance is the fraction of adjacency-matrix entries that must change, and each vertex subset supporting the pattern is counted once.
The target is matching constant-factor bounds in both the graph order and the proximity parameter, with constants allowed to depend on the pattern.
The removal lemma guarantees positive density at every fixed distance, but the general quantitative bounds remain widely separated.
Sharp bounds would quantify the worst-case visibility of local violations and the sampling cost of detecting them.

definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(t=|V(H)|\). All graphs are undirected and have neither loops nor multiple edges. A graph is \(H\)-free if there is no injective map \(\phi:V(H)\to V(G)\) taking every edge of \(H\) to an edge of \(G\); nonedges of \(H\) impose no restriction. Let \(r_H(G)\) be the least number of edges that must be deleted from \(G\) to make it \(H\)-free. Allowing edge additions as well cannot decrease this minimum. Use the source's adjacency-matrix distance \(d_H(G)=2r_H(G)/n^{2}\): each changed undirected edge changes two matrix entries. Say that \(G\) is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\), with a strict inequality. Define \(N_H(G)\) to be the number of \(t\)-element subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\) for which \(G[S]\) contains an ordinary copy of \(H\), counting each such subset once even if it supports several embeddings. This fixes the copy convention suggested by the source's random-subset test; counting injective labelled embeddings instead changes the count by factors between one and \(t!\). A feasible pair is a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and an integer \(n\ge t\) for which at least one graph on \([n]\) has \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\). On precisely this domain, set \[M_H(\varepsilon,n)=\min\{N_H(G):V(G)=[n],\ d_H(G)>\varepsilon\}.\] The minimum is over a nonempty finite set, so it is a positive integer. No value is requested for an infeasible pair. The constants in the matching bounds may depend on the whole fixed pattern \(H\), but not on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\); in particular, \(\varepsilon\) may decrease with \(n\). The target is the growth of this extremal function, not the running time of enumerating graphs. No extra minimum-degree, regularity, randomness or sparsity promise is imposed on \(G\).
answer_criterion: Supply the matching asymptotic bounds in the formal statement and a complete Lean-checked proof of both inequalities for every permitted pattern and feasible parameter pair. The lower inequality must hold for every graph at the stated distance, and the upper inequality must establish existence of graphs with the claimed copy count. Merely restating the defining minimization, tabulating finitely many values, giving one-sided bounds, or establishing only that some positive removal bound exists does not meet this growth target. The precision here is a multiplicative constant factor depending only on the pattern, not additive \(1/100\) accuracy on a normalized copy density.

context_blocks.text: For a fixed pattern on \(t\) vertices, a random \(t\)-vertex subset detects a violation with probability exactly \(N_H(G)/\binom{n}{t}\). The extremal function asks how small that probability can be while repairing the whole graph still requires changing a positive fraction of its adjacency matrix. This connects a global repair requirement to the frequency of small observable witnesses.

Ordinary and induced removal are different questions. An ordinary copy only requires the pattern's edges to be present; an induced copy also requires its nonedges to remain absent. For example, three mutually adjacent vertices contain a three-vertex path as an ordinary subgraph, but not as an induced path. This card retains ordinary copies from Definition 8.16 and the connected-pattern scope of Open Problem 8.17.

The classical removal lemma ensures a positive copy density for every fixed positive distance, uniformly over graph order. Its quantitative content can nevertheless be extremely weak: the known general lower guarantee involves an inverse tower of exponentials, while nonbipartite examples exclude every fixed polynomial dependence on distance. A positive constant for each fixed distance therefore says much less than a sharp answer as the distance tends to zero.

The source asks for relatively tight bounds on a function of both distance and graph order. This card makes that precision explicit as constant-factor matching bounds with pattern-dependent constants, retaining both parameters and specifying the feasible domain. It does not silently replace the question by the triangle-only case, by a large-graph limit, or by the already known polynomial/nonpolynomial classification. The matrix normalization differs by a factor of two from the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention in several later papers.

The dependence on the host graph matters. A sufficiently large minimum degree can give linear removal bounds for cliques, whereas unrestricted hosts admit much smaller copy densities. Such a theorem clarifies a special regime and cannot supply a bound for every graph in the domain of this card.

source_formulation.text: Goldreich, Open Problem 8.17, asks for relatively tight bounds on the minimum number of copies of a connected fixed graph in a graph far from ordinary subgraph-freeness. The constant-factor precision and finite feasible-domain conventions are explicit editorial specifications of that quantitative request.
